title: SPECIAL EDITION 02 — Why We Must Keep Thinking

image.alt: A person bends over a notebook and writes by hand, showing the act of forming and recording thought even when faster answers are available.

slides.text:
Why we must
keep thinking

Thinking is not merely a cost paid until an answer appears. It is the process through which we become people able to judge what to believe and choose.

image.alt: A person draws repeated lines and forms in a sketchbook with a pencil, representing the capacity built through correction and iteration.

slides.text:
Process is not disposable
once a result arrives

As people compare, fail, and try again, they learn how to frame a problem and check their own work. The finished result is not the only thing that remains; so does the ability to face the next problem.

If faster results cost us that ability, efficiency may be not pure progress but an exchange for something important.

image.alt: A person studies multiple notes attached to a glass wall, representing the work of comparing answers, questioning evidence, and forming judgment.

slides.text:
Thinking builds
your own criteria

Judgment is different from possessing many correct answers. It is the ability to compare possibilities, question evidence, revisit why something failed, and decide what to trust and what to reject.

Only through that experience do we develop internal criteria for evaluating whether an answer from another person—or an AI—fits the situation before us.

image.alt: Several people hold notebooks and pens while discussing their reasoning, representing the work of explaining and taking responsibility for a decision.

slides.text:
Answers can be borrowed.
Responsibility cannot.

Responsibility means more than accepting blame when a result is wrong. It means explaining why a choice was made, what was given up, and where judgment must begin again.

Only someone who has constructed the reasons for a decision can become the author of its consequences.

image.alt: A person compares several printed documents beside a laptop, showing the separation between a tool's output and human review.

slides.text:
Divide what AI can do
from what humans must retain

AI can take on search, drafting, repetitive work, and finding counterexamples.

People should retain the question, the criteria for choosing, fact-checking, and final responsibility. The goal is not to work without AI, but to prevent __the speed of a tool from deciding the purpose of a life__.

image.alt:
Now that answers arrive faster,
__which questions__ should I
still work through myself?

slides.text:

still work through myself?

caption.body: Thinking is not merely a cost paid until an answer appears. Through comparison, doubt, and revision, people build the criteria by which they decide what to believe and choose. AI can search, draft, and propose counterexamples. But if we also surrender the question, the criteria, verification, and final decision, a result may remain while our capacity to become its author weakens.
